content: The 2010 study published in the International Journal for Parasitology (Volume 40, Issue 5, Pages 515–519) by French MD and colleagues focused on the school-based control of urinary schistosomiasis in Zanzibar, Tanzania. The researchers utilized reagent strips to monitor micro-haematuria as a rapid urological assessment tool. In 2007, Massa K and colleagues explored community perceptions regarding community-directed treatment and school-based approaches for controlling schistosomiasis and soil-transmitted helminthiasis among school-aged children in Lushoto District, Tanzania. This study, published in the Journal of Biosocial Science (Volume 41, Issue 1, Pages 89–105), compared the effectiveness of these two approaches in reducing the prevalence and intensity of these infections. Brooker S, Clements AC, and Bundy DAP, in their 2006 review in Advances in Parasitology (Volume 62, Pages 221–261), provided a comprehensive analysis of the global epidemiology, ecology, and control strategies for soil-transmitted helminth infections. Mohammed KA and colleagues conducted a safety study in 2008 on the triple co-administration of ivermectin, albendazole, and praziquantel in Zanzibar. Their findings, published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases (Volume 2, Issue 1, Article e171), demonstrated the safety of this combination therapy. Olsen A, in a 2007 article in the Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (Volume 101, Issue 8, Pages 747–758), evaluated the efficacy and safety of various drug combinations for treating schistosomiasis, soil-transmitted helminthiasis, lymphatic filariasis, and onchocerciasis. Bundy DA and colleagues, in their 2009 publication in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases (Volume 3, Issue 1, Article e362), emphasized the importance of asking the right questions to optimize deworming programs and their developmental impact. Smits HL, in a 2009 review in the Expert Review of Anti-infective Therapy (Volume 7, Issue 1, Pages 37–56), discussed the prospects of controlling neglected tropical diseases through mass drug administration. Churcher TS and Basáñez MG, in their 2009 article in Trends in Parasitology (Volume 25, Issue 1, Pages 11–17), proposed sampling strategies to detect suboptimal responses to ivermectin in the treatment of river blindness (onchocerciasis). Mathieu E and colleagues, in a 2003 study published in the Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (Volume 97, Issue 5, Pages 501–505), compared methods for estimating drug coverage in filariasis elimination programs in Leogane Commune, Haiti. Geary TG and colleagues, in their 2010 review in the International Journal for Parasitology (Volume 40, Issue 1, Pages 1–13), highlighted unresolved issues in the pharmacology of anthelmintics for human helminth infections. Ramaiah KD, in a 2009 article in Trends in Parasitology (Volume 25, Issue 1, Pages 7–8), reviewed the progress and challenges of India's lymphatic filariasis elimination program. Wanjí S and colleagues, in a 2009 study in Parasites & Vectors (Volume 2, Article 39), examined the community-directed delivery of doxycycline for treating onchocerciasis in areas co-endemic with loiasis in Cameroon. Diawara A and colleagues, in a 2009 publication in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases (Volume 3, Issue 3, Article e397), developed assays to detect beta-tubulin codon 200 polymorphism in Trichuris trichiura and Ascaris lumbricoides. McManus DP and Loukas A, in their 2008 review in Clinical Microbiology Reviews (Volume 21, Issue 1, Pages 225–242), provided an update on the current status of vaccines for schistosomiasis. Doenhoff MJ and colleagues, in a 2009 chapter in Antimicrobial Drug Resistance (Volume 1, Pages 629–646), discussed chemotherapy and drug resistance in schistosomiasis, fascioliasis, and tapeworm infections. Lightowlers MW, in a 2004 article in Developments in Biologicals (Volume 119, Pages 361–368), reviewed vaccination strategies for preventing cysticercosis. The WHO Technical Report Series No. 972 (2012) outlined research priorities for helminth infections, as determined by the TDR Disease Reference Group on Helminth Infections. Keiser J and Utzinger J, in a 2008 systematic review and meta-analysis published in the Journal of the American Medical Association (Volume 299, Issue 16, Pages 1937–1948), evaluated the efficacy of current drugs against soil-transmitted helminth infections. Stepek G and colleagues, in a 2006 article in the International Journal of Experimental Pathology (Volume 87, Issue 5, Pages 325–341), questioned whether new control methods are required for human gastrointestinal nematode infections. Hu Y, Xiao SH, and Aroian RV, in a 2009 study in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases (Volume 3, Issue 8, Article e499), identified tribendimidine as an L-type nicotinic acetylcholine receptor agonist with potential as a new anthelmintic. Wolstenholme AJ and colleagues, in a 2004 review in Trends in Parasitology (Volume 20, Issue 10, Pages 469–476), discussed drug resistance in veterinary helminths. Martin PJ, Anderson N, and Jarrett RG, in a 1989 study in the Australian Veterinary Journal (Volume 66, Issue 8, Pages 236–240), evaluated methods for detecting benzimidazole resistance using fecal egg count reduction tests and in vitro assays. De Clercq D and colleagues, in a 1997 study in the American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (Volume 57, Issue 1, Pages 25–30), reported the failure of mebendazole in treating human hookworm infections in southern Mali.
